title.narrative: Fair trade for African Blackwood: achieving self-sufficiency - phase 1

description.narrative: The project will reduce poverty amongst forest dependent communities in SE Tanzania, through developing fair trade for African Blackwood from community-owned forests. Communities previously received ~0.01% of export value of the world’s most valuable timber (used in musical instruments such as clarinets, oboes and bagpipes). Communities who collectively and sustainably manage their forests can retain licence fees ~400 times greater. However, illegal logging is rife; communities need to be able to securely label timber coming from their forests; forest certification is a mechanism to do this. At the supply end the project will continue to invest in supporting rural communities in Tanzania to set aside and manage their forests sustainably, and to meet the standards of forest certification. At the demand end, this project is engaging directly with the market in woodwind instruments, which is worth an estimated £35m in UK alone, by creating demand for a new product variant, made from certified blackwood from community-managed forests. Under this continuation project marketing of African Blackwood and other timbers from community-managed forests to instrument manufacturers and consumers through the Sound & Fair campaign will intensify. The project will continue to engage with manufacturers of musical instruments made from African Blackwood, beginning with classical woodwind. Rising consumer awareness and new legislation in the US and EU, requiring greater transparency over the supply source and guarantees of legality, will dramatically increase demand for FSC-certified timber. The project partners estimate that by the end of the project at least 3,000 musical instruments made from timber from community managed forests will either be under manufacture or already sold. In revenue terms, this amounts to sales of between £2.5m and £5m, with a further £5m to £10m in the pipeline, though it is likely to be higher still. The increase in awareness these sales will provide, supported by a marketing campaign, is expected to further boost demand for this product. Increasing penetration of this product into the UK woodwind market should lead to greater international interest and support later diversification of both products and species. Higher demand will allow communities in Tanzania to increase prices further; communities could potentially earn up to £50,000 per year from their forests. The project assists communities in managing this revenue in a fair and equitable manner. This next phase of the project will begin the transition to financial sustainability and self-sufficiency by commencing charging forest communities token fees for services they receive in support of PFM and for the administration of the FSC group certificate. The resulting conservation of forest cover will help the global fight against and increase communities’ resilience to climate change.
